docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Researchers look for funding across thousands of university, government and foundation websites. Most of what they find is irrelevant, and much of what looks relevant is closed to them: it requires a different nationality, career stage or host country. Existing scholarly recommender systems rank opportunities by topic; they do not check eligibility, and they do not verify that the facts they display are correct.

ACCESS is a multi-agent AI system that addresses both problems. It builds a library of funding programmes from the open web, verifies every displayed fact against the funder's own page, and returns only the programmes a researcher is eligible for, ranked by fit and with the evidence for each decision.

The design rests on one division of labour: language models read; deterministic code decides. Models are good at reading messy web pages and judging whether a sentence supports a claim. Code is better at decisions that must be reproducible and explainable, such as whether a researcher meets a nationality rule.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
ACCESS covers research funding: scholarships from undergraduate to PhD level, research fellowships, postdoctoral positions, research grants and travel grants. Coverage priority goes to the destinations with the most student traffic: Singapore, the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, China (including Hong Kong), Australia, Canada and the rest of Europe.

ACCESS supports discovery and decision-making only. It does not submit applications or contact funders on a user's behalf, because doing so would transfer decision-making agency from the researcher to the system and raise questions of safety and accountability.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
A researcher looking for funding faces three difficulties at once.

The result is a familiar experience for postgraduate students: hours spent across many tabs, reading fine print, and still not knowing which opportunities are realistically open to them.

docs.title: The information is fragmented
docs.text: Scholarships, fellowships and grants are published on thousands of university, government and foundation websites. No single portal covers them, and aggregator sites are often incomplete or out of date.

docs.title: Eligibility, not topic, decides
docs.text: Nationality, career stage, degree, host country and deadline determine whether an application is possible at all. Search engines and scholarly recommenders rank by topical relevance and leave these rules to the reader.

docs.title: Errors are costly
docs.text: A misread nationality rule or a wrong deadline can cost an applicant weeks of preparation. General-purpose language models make such errors fluently, so every fact shown to a researcher must be checkable.

docs.title: Our vision
docs.text:
We want a researcher to describe themselves once and receive a shortlist they can trust: only the programmes they are eligible for, ranked by how well each fits their goals, with every decision traceable to a sentence on the funder's own page.

Four principles guide the design.

Principle What it means in ACCESS Official sources only Programmes are read from funders' own websites. Aggregators are used to discover programmes, never as the source of a fact. Eligibility as a hard constraint Plain, tested code applies every eligibility rule to the researcher's profile. The same profile always receives the same answer. Every claim is verified Three AI judges from three different companies check each extracted claim against the page, and an auditor measures how many planted errors they catch. Claims that cannot be confirmed are withheld. Models read, code decides Language models do what they do well, reading messy pages and judging whether a sentence supports a claim. Decisions that must be reproducible are left to code.

ACCESS supports discovery and decision-making only. It does not submit applications or contact funders on a researcher's behalf, because doing so would transfer agency from the researcher to the system and raise questions of accountability.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text: ACCESS is designed for people at the transition points of an academic career: an undergraduate looking for a funded master's degree, a master's student seeking a PhD scholarship, a doctoral candidate looking for a postdoctoral fellowship, and early-career researchers looking for grants and travel funding.

docs.title: Where it stands, and where it is going
docs.text:
The prototype covers 629 verified programmes with 1,009 quoted eligibility rules, drawn from funders in 30 host countries. First results appear in under half a second, and 93% of benchmark searches find the target programme in the top five. The Results and Test report pages give the measurements in full.

The next steps follow from the limitations we have measured:

  • Coverage. Continental Europe is under-represented, so national European schemes are the next priority.
  • Evaluation. A comparison with a relevance-only baseline will quantify how much the eligibility gate improves on topic matching alone.
  • Scope. In the longer term, the same verified, eligibility-aware approach can extend from funding to supervisors, conferences and career opportunities, towards a single platform for the postgraduate journey.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Plain-language explanations of the terms used on this site, with an everyday analogy where one helps. Many of these terms also show a short definition when you hover over them elsewhere on the site.

docs.title: AI and language models
docs.text: Language model (LLM) A program trained on large amounts of text to predict and generate language. It can read a web page, answer questions about it and write text, but it can also state things that are not true. Like a very well-read assistant who answers fluently, but whose work still needs checking. Pretrained model A model trained once by its developer and then used as is. ACCESS trains no models; it only gives instructions (prompts) to existing ones. Zero-shot Asking a model to do a task from instructions alone, without giving it worked examples. Like handing a new colleague a blank form and the instructions, without a filled-in sample. Hallucination A fluent, confident statement by a language model that is not supported by its source. Like a witness filling gaps in their memory with plausible details. Agent, multi-agent system An agent is a program that carries out one job on its own, repeatedly. A multi-agent system divides a large task among several agents. In ACCESS, the agents (Scout, Scraper, Critic, Auditor, Sentinel) each do one job. Like an assembly line where each station does one step. Workflow A system whose steps follow fixed paths set by its designers, as opposed to an autonomous agent that chooses its own steps. ACCESS is a workflow, because predictability matters more than autonomy when deciding eligibility. Neuro-symbolic A design that combines neural models (good at language and patterns) with symbolic code (good at exact logic). In ACCESS, language models read and judge; code decides eligibility. Like a translator working with an accountant: one interprets, the other does the sums. Token, quota, free tier Models process text in small pieces called tokens. Free tiers limit how many tokens or requests each user may send per minute and per day (the quota). ACCESS uses free tiers only, so quotas set its speed. Deterministic Always giving the same output for the same input. The eligibility gate is deterministic; a language model is not.

docs.title: Collecting and extracting data
docs.text: Crawler, crawling A program that visits web pages and follows their links to find more pages. Like a librarian walking the shelves, noting every book and every reference it points to. robots.txt A file in which a website states which pages automated programs may visit. ACCESS respects it. Headless browser A web browser without a visible window, controlled by a program. It is needed for pages whose content only appears after JavaScript runs. Fingerprint (hash) A short code computed from a page's text. Identical text always gives the same code, so duplicates are found by comparing codes rather than whole pages. Like comparing fingerprints instead of whole people. Schema A fixed list of fields, each with a defined type, that every record must follow (for example, deadline as a date, amount as a number with a currency). Like a standard application form: every programme is described in the same boxes. Evidence quote, grounding The exact sentence from the funder's page that supports an extracted fact. A fact is grounded if its quote is found on the page. Like a footnote that lets you check the claim yourself. Cascade Running cheap steps on everything and expensive steps only on what remains. Like airport security: everyone walks through the scanner, only a few bags are opened. Blackboard architecture Agents coordinate through a shared store of data instead of calling each other. Like colleagues working from one shared whiteboard: anyone can step away without stopping the others. Max-min fairness Always serving the group that currently has the least. ACCESS crawls next for the priority country with the fewest verified programmes.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: LLM-as-a-judge Using a language model to evaluate whether a statement is correct or supported. Judge panel, ensemble, majority vote Several judges vote independently and the majority decides. ACCESS uses three judges from three different companies. Like three referees from different leagues: one referee's blind spot is outvoted by the other two. Echo chamber When the checker shares the blind spots of the thing it checks, for example a model judging its own output. Avoided by using different companies for extraction, judging and auditing. Claim, claim decomposition A claim is one checkable fact, such as "the deadline is 2 June". Decomposition splits a record into separate claims so each can be verified on its own. Like marking an exam question by question rather than giving one overall grade. Locate, then interpret The two steps of the claim check. Locate: code checks that the date, amount or quote actually appears on the page. Interpret: judges read only that passage and decide whether it supports the claim. Fail closed When unsure, withhold rather than guess. An unconfirmed fact is shown as "not stated". Like a door that locks, rather than opens, when the power fails. Fault injection, mutation testing Deliberately inserting known errors to measure whether a checking process catches them. Like a fire drill, or a test parcel sent through airport security to check that the scanner works. Negative control A test where the correct outcome is known to be "no", used to check that a change has not made a test too lenient. ACCESS fed deliberately wrong amounts to the reworded amount check: only 1 of 28 was accepted. Fleiss' kappa (κ) A measure of agreement among several raters that corrects for agreement expected by chance. 0 means chance-level agreement, 1 means perfect agreement; 0.41–0.60 is conventionally "moderate". Trust score A weighted score summarising how well a record is supported: source authenticity, judge votes, grounding and agreement.

docs.title: Search and matching
docs.text: Embedding A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Texts with similar meaning have similar numbers. Like map coordinates for meaning: related ideas sit close together. Vector index A store of embeddings that can be searched for the ones closest to a query. Cosine similarity A measure of how closely two embeddings point in the same direction; used as the similarity between two texts. Keyword search, BM25 Search by matching words, weighting rare words more than common ones. BM25 is the standard formula. Like the index at the back of a book. Dense search Search by comparing embeddings, so it also finds text that says the same thing in different words. Hybrid search, reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) Running keyword and dense search together and merging their ranked lists. RRF merges lists by rank position, so the two searches' scores need not be on the same scale. Like combining two judges' rankings by placing, not by their different scoring systems. Recall@k The share of searches whose correct answer appears in the top k results. Recall@5 = 0.93 means 93 of 100 test searches found the target programme in the top five. MRR (mean reciprocal rank) The average of 1 / (position of the correct answer). It rewards putting the correct answer near the top. Known-item benchmark A search test in which each query has exactly one known correct answer, so no human relevance judgements are needed. Precision, recall (of a filter) Precision: of the items the filter kept, how many were right. Recall: of all the right items, how many the filter kept. A fishing net: precision is how much of the catch is fish; recall is how many of the fish you caught. Confidence interval (95% CI) A range that, under the method's assumptions, contains the true value in 95% of repeated samples. Wide intervals signal small samples.

docs.title: Eligibility and ranking
docs.text: Eligibility gate, constraint satisfaction Checking each rule of a programme against the profile, one at a time, with code. Like a checklist at a border: every item must be satisfied, and each refusal names the item. Hard rule, soft rule A hard rule excludes outright if not met (for example, nationality). A soft rule allows a small, closable gap (for example, a language score slightly below the requirement). Near miss, gap cost A programme the researcher misses only on soft rules. The gap cost estimates the effort, in weeks, to close the gap. Information gain How much a piece of information reduces uncertainty. ACCESS asks the one follow-up question that settles the most "unknown" eligibility checks. Like the best first question in "Twenty Questions". Late fusion Combining two separately computed scores into one final score. ACCESS uses 0.7 × fit score + 0.3 × similarity. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) Answering a question by first retrieving relevant passages and then having the model answer only from them, with citations. An open-book exam: the answer must come from the book, with page numbers. Faithfulness Whether an answer's quotes and citations really come from the source. ACCESS checks every quote against the page.

docs.title: Threats to validity
docs.text:
• Sample sizes. Benchmarks use 100 queries and small pilots; confidence intervals are wide, and differences within overlapping intervals are not claimed as significant.
  • Synthetic queries. Benchmark queries are generated from the same text that is indexed, which can favour keyword matching. Results are relative comparisons, not absolute search quality.
  • Coverage bias. The library reflects which sites were reachable and processed first.
  • Hand-set parameters. Trust weights, gap-cost estimates and the 0.7 / 0.3 ranking weights are expert choices, not learned.

docs.text:
Work in progress

The ACCESS app is a working prototype under active development. This report records the state of the demonstration build tested on 12 October 2026. Figures will change as the verified library grows.

Run: 12 October 2026, 06:26 SGT · Suite: 49 automated tests in 12 areas Library under test: 373 claim-verified programmes · Status of the app: work in progress (demo build)

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
Tests run 49, in 12 areas Passed 48 Failed 1 (D2: three of fourteen test profiles receive fewer than five results; a coverage gap, not a logic error) Defects found and fixed while preparing and running the suite 10 in the app, 3 in the test suite itself (Section 5) Wall-clock time 31 s with warm caches; about 2 min when the AI services are called afresh

The core promise of the app holds in every test: every programme shown matches the researcher's chosen country, funding type and career stage, every displayed eligibility rule is quoted from the funder's official page, and the same input always gives the same answer. The remaining weakness is coverage: some combinations (for example a master's degree in Japan, or mid-career research grants) return only one to four programmes because few verified programmes exist for them yet.

docs.title: 2. Scope and method
docs.text:
The suite tests the app as a user meets it (the four pages and the search form) and the components behind it (eligibility gate, search library, retrieval, AI ranking, question answering, application plans). Three kinds of test are used:

  • Example-based tests compare an output with a known correct answer (for example, 37 hand-checked eligibility cases).
  • Property and integrity tests check a statement that must hold for every item (for example, "every rule's quote appears on the official page", checked for all 633 rules).
  • Metamorphic tests compare related searches when the correct answer for one search is unknown. If a researcher adds a country, no result for the countries already chosen may disappear. Such relations expose logic errors without a labelled ground truth.

Fourteen realistic researcher profiles are used across the suite: the four example researchers on the home page and ten new ones that vary nationality, career stage, field, destination and funding type (Appendix A).

The AI tests (H to J) use the free-tier models deployed in the app. Their outputs are cached, so repeated runs are fast and reproducible, and latencies reported for them come from the first, uncached run.

docs.title: 4. Known limitations
docs.text:
1. Coverage (D2): a few combinations return one to four programmes. The library holds 373 verified programmes and grows as the critic verifies the backlog.

docs.title: Documentation overview
docs.text:
This section describes ACCESS layer by layer. Each component is documented in the same way:

  • What it does, in one or two sentences.
  • Method: the concept or algorithm used.
  • Why this method: the alternatives considered, including the state of the art, and the trade-off we accepted.
  • Evidence: a measurement showing whether it works, and where it fails.

New to the field? How it works, explained introduces every method in plain language first, then with its equation and a worked example using the system's real numbers.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
ACCESS was designed around four objectives:

  1. A reliable repository. Collect and structure funding opportunities from heterogeneous web sources, with every displayed fact verified.
  2. Researcher profiles. Capture research interests, background and eligibility attributes from consent-based input.
  3. Constraint-aware filtering. Exclude opportunities the researcher is not eligible for, while keeping "near misses" whose gap could realistically be closed.
  4. Fit ranking and evaluation. Rank eligible opportunities by fit with the researcher, and compare the approach against a relevance-only baseline.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
ACCESS is a neuro-symbolic, multi-agent workflow. Language models read, judge and write; deterministic code searches, decides eligibility and scores. No model is trained: all models are pretrained and used through prompts or embeddings, on free tiers or run locally.

    N --> C[Info Critic<br/>3-company panel + claim check]
    C --> V[(Vector index)]
    C --> R[(Rule register)]
    A[Auditor<br/>planted errors] -.tests.-> C
  end

  end

  end

docs.title: Three design principles
docs.text:
Cascade. Cheap operations run on everything; expensive ones run on the few items that remain. A free keyword filter discards most web pages before any language model reads them, and model reasoning is applied only to the candidates that survive filtering. This matters because free model quotas, not computing power, limit the system.

Independence. No model checks its own work. The model that extracts facts (Google Gemini) comes from a different company than the three judges that verify them, and the auditor that tests the judges never grades its own votes. Language-model evaluators are known to favour their own outputs [12], and errors that are independent cancel out under a majority vote, while correlated errors do not [11].

Fail closed. A fact that cannot be confirmed is withheld and shown as "not stated, see the official page", never guessed. An error therefore becomes a missing value rather than a wrong one.

docs.title: How the agents work together
docs.text:
The background agents never call each other directly. They read and write one shared database (a blackboard architecture), so each agent can be stopped, restarted or scaled independently without affecting the others.

Agent Role Scout Finds websites to crawl: curated seeds, ranked universities, national agencies, links found while crawling Scraper Crawls sites, renders pages built by JavaScript, and runs the Normalizer on candidate pages Critic Verifies each record with a three-company judge panel and the claim check, then publishes verified records Auditor Tests the Critic by planting known errors and by blind re-reading of random pages Sentinel Monitors progress every five minutes and applies a whitelisted set of safe fixes, such as restarting an agent

docs.title: How it works, explained
docs.text:
This page explains the methods inside ACCESS for readers from any background. Every section has three levels, and you can stop at whichever suits you:

In plain words

The idea in everyday language, with an analogy where one helps.

Worked example

The method applied to a small, concrete case, with the actual numbers.

The maths sits between the two, with every symbol explained. All constants on this page are the values the deployed system uses, and each section links to the layer page where the method is evaluated.

docs.text:
Before the individual methods, here is what happens between pressing Find funding and reading the results. The first answer comes from local code alone; language models only refine it afterwards.

docs.title: 1 · Turning text into numbers: embeddings
docs.text:
In plain words

A computer cannot compare the meaning of two sentences directly, so we convert each text into a list of numbers, called an embedding, in which texts with similar meanings receive similar numbers. Think of it as giving every text a position on a map with 768 directions instead of two: "PhD scholarship in machine learning" and "doctoral fellowship in artificial intelligence" land close together even though they share almost no words, while "grant for music performance" lands far away.

"PhD scholarship in machine learning" "doctoral fellowship in AI" "grant for music performance" small angle θ: similar meaning orange arc, large angle: different meaning

The maths. We measure closeness by the angle between two embedding vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\), using cosine similarity:

\[ \cos\theta \;=\; \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\lVert\mathbf{a}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{b}\rVert} \;=\; \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{768} a_i b_i}{\sqrt{\sum_i a_i^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_i b_i^2}} \]

The result runs from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to 1 (same direction). We store every vector already divided by its length, so at search time the similarity is a single dot product, \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\), and comparing a query with every programme in the library takes milliseconds.

Worked example

With toy three-number embeddings \(\mathbf{a} = (0.8, 0.6, 0)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (0.6, 0.8, 0)\), both of length 1: \(\cos\theta = 0.8 \times 0.6 + 0.6 \times 0.8 + 0 = 0.96\), very similar. Against \(\mathbf{c} = (0, 0, 1)\): \(\cos\theta = 0\), unrelated.

Where ACCESS uses it. The model is nomic-embed-text, run locally, which produces 768 numbers per text. Programme descriptions are embedded once when they are published; the researcher's query is embedded at search time. See Layer 2.

docs.title: 2 · Keyword search: BM25
docs.text:
In plain words

Embeddings are good at meaning but can blur exact names: "Chevening", "SINGA" or "cryo-EM" matter precisely. BM25 is the classic keyword-scoring method behind many search engines. It rewards a programme for containing the words in your query, with three sensible adjustments: rare words count for more than common ones, repeating a word helps less and less, and long pages do not win merely by being long.

The maths. For a query \(q\) and a programme description \(d\):

\[ \text{BM25}(d, q) \;=\; \sum_{t \in q} \text{IDF}(t)\cdot \frac{f(t,d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(t,d) + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\dfrac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)} \]

where the weight of a word, its inverse document frequency, is

\[ \text{IDF}(t) \;=\; \ln\!\left(1 + \frac{N - n(t) + 0.5}{n(t) + 0.5}\right) \] Symbol Meaning Value in ACCESS \(f(t,d)\) how many times word \(t\) appears in description \(d\) counted \(\lvert d\rvert\), avgdl length of \(d\), and the average length across the library counted \(N\), \(n(t)\) number of programmes, and how many contain \(t\) counted \(k_1\) how quickly repeated words stop helping (saturation) 1.5 \(b\) how strongly long descriptions are penalised (0 = not at all, 1 = fully) 0.75

Worked example: the three adjustments

  • Rare words count more. In a library of 1,000 programmes, a word found in 5 of them has \(\text{IDF} = \ln(1 + 995.5/5.5) \approx 5.20\); a word found in 600 has \(\text{IDF} \approx 0.51\). The rare word is worth about ten times as much.
  • Repetition saturates. For a description of average length, the word-count part of the formula is \(f \cdot 2.5 / (f + 1.5)\): one mention gives 1.00, two give 1.43, five give 1.92, twenty give 2.33, and no number of repetitions can exceed 2.5.
  • Length is normalised. A description twice the average length needs more mentions to reach the same score.

Where ACCESS uses it. Matching programmes to a researcher (Layer 2), and finding the passages of an official page that relate to a claim or a question (Layers 0 and 3). We implemented it directly from the formula above.

docs.title: 3 · Combining two rankings: reciprocal rank fusion
docs.text:
In plain words

We now have two ranked lists, one by meaning and one by keywords, and their scores are on different scales: a cosine of 0.6 and a BM25 score of 14 cannot be added. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) ignores the raw scores and uses only each programme's position in each list. A programme near the top of either list scores well; one near the top of both scores best.

The maths. For each programme \(d\), with \(\text{rank}_r(d)\) its position in list \(r\) (1 = top):

\[ \text{RRF}(d) \;=\; \sum_{r} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)}, \qquad k = 60,\quad w_{\text{keyword}} = 2,\quad w_{\text{meaning}} = 1 \]

The constant \(k = 60\) comes from the original paper [18] and stops the very top positions from dominating. The 2:1 weighting in favour of keywords was chosen on our known-item benchmark, where it found the target programme in the top five for 93% of queries, against 88% for keywords alone and 73% for meaning alone.

Worked example

Programme Rank by meaning Rank by keywords RRF score A 1 3 \(\frac{1}{61} + \frac{2}{63} = 0.04814\) B 4 1 \(\frac{1}{64} + \frac{2}{61} = \mathbf{0.04841}\) C 2 10 \(\frac{1}{62} + \frac{2}{70} = 0.04470\)

B finishes first: it is the strongest keyword match and still reasonable on meaning. C is close in meaning but shares few of the query's words, so it drops to third.

docs.title: 4 · Guessing research fields: zero-shot classification
docs.text:
In plain words

The researcher writes a free-text description; the eligibility rules need fields such as "computer science" or "life sciences". Instead of training a classifier, we embed the description and the name of each of 24 fields, and keep the fields whose embeddings are closest. "Zero-shot" means no labelled training examples are needed.

The maths. With \(s_j\) the cosine similarity between the description and field \(j\), we keep every field within a small margin of the best:

\[ \text{fields} \;=\; \{\, j \;:\; s_j \ge \max_i s_i - 0.035 \,\}, \quad \text{at most 4, best first} \]

The margin exists because descriptions often span two areas. With only the single best field, one physicist's description was labelled chemistry, because physics scored just below it; with the margin, both are kept. The researcher can always confirm or change the fields. See Layer 1.

docs.title: 5 · Eligibility as logic: the gate
docs.text:
In plain words

Whether you can apply is a yes-or-no question with a reason, so we answer it with plain, tested code rather than a language model. Each programme's rules (nationality, career stage, years since PhD, language scores and so on) are stored as small typed statements, each with the quote it came from. The gate checks each rule against your profile, the same way every time.

Every rule is a triple, attribute · operator · value, for example nationality in [Singapore, Singapore PR] or ielts gte 6.5. Checking one rule follows this decision path:

flowchart LR
  A[Rule from the register] --> B{Is the attribute<br/>in the profile?}
  B -- no --> U[Unknown<br/>shown as 'to confirm']
  B -- yes --> C{Rule met?}
  C -- yes --> P[Pass]
  C -- no --> D{Soft rule, and the gap<br/>within the margin?}
  D -- yes --> N[Near]
  D -- no --> F[Fail]

A programme's overall outcome then follows from its rules:

\[ \text{outcome} = \begin{cases} \text{excluded} & \text{if any rule fails}\\ \text{within reach} & \text{else if any rule is near}\\ \text{eligible} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

An unknown rule never counts as a pass: the result card marks it "to confirm", and the follow-up question (section 6) asks for the missing fact.

Near-miss margins. Only soft rules can be near. Hard rules, such as nationality or age, either pass or fail.

Soft rule Counts as near if you are short by at most IELTS 1.0 band TOEFL 15 points GPA 0.3 Publications 2 Work experience 1 year

Ordering near misses. Within-reach programmes are ordered by an estimated effort to close the gap, the gap cost, in weeks:

\[ \text{gap cost} \;=\; \sum_{\text{near rules}} \frac{\text{required} - \text{yours}}{\text{step}} \times \text{weeks per step} \]

with steps of 0.5 IELTS band (4 weeks), 5 TOEFL points (4 weeks), 0.1 GPA (8 weeks), one publication (12 weeks) and one year of work experience (52 weeks). A missing career stage or degree counts as 26 weeks.

Worked example

A programme asks for IELTS 7.0 and you have 6.5: the gap is 0.5, within the 1.0 margin, so the rule is near. Gap cost \(= 0.5 / 0.5 \times 4 = 4\) weeks. A second programme asking for GPA 3.6 when you have 3.4 costs \(0.2 / 0.1 \times 8 = 16\) weeks, so the IELTS programme is listed first.

The weeks are deliberately coarse; they are used only to put the easiest gaps first. See Layer 2.

docs.title: 6 · One follow-up question: greedy information gain
docs.text:
In plain words

If many results say "to confirm: years since PhD", one answer settles all of them at once. ACCESS asks the single question that would settle the most open checks across your results, instead of a long questionnaire.

The maths. With \(U(a)\) the number of unknown checks across the shown results that depend on attribute \(a\):

\[ a^{*} \;=\; \arg\max_{a}\; U(a) \]

Each unknown check is an uncertain outcome, so the attribute behind the most unknowns removes the most uncertainty per question. This is a greedy, count-based approximation of information gain: it does not weigh how uncertain each check is, which keeps it deterministic, instant and easy to explain.

docs.title: 7 · The fit score: late fusion
docs.text:
In plain words

Once the gate has decided which programmes you can apply for, a language model reads each one alongside your profile and gives a fit score from 0 to 100 with a one-sentence reason. We blend that judgement with the meaning-based similarity from section 1, so the order reflects both a reasoned opinion and a measurable match.

The maths. First the cosine similarity is stretched onto 0–100, so that 0.3 becomes 0 and 0.8 becomes 100, with values outside that range clipped:

\[ \text{sim}_{100} \;=\; \min\!\left(100,\; \max\!\left(0,\; \frac{\cos\theta - 0.3}{0.5} \times 100\right)\right) \]

Then the two are combined:

\[ \text{score} \;=\; 0.7 \times \text{fit} \;+\; 0.3 \times \text{sim}_{100} \]

Worked example

The model gives a programme a fit of 90; its cosine similarity to the query is 0.62. \(\text{sim}_{100} = (0.62 - 0.3)/0.5 \times 100 = 64\), so \(\text{score} = 0.7 \times 90 + 0.3 \times 64 = 63 + 19.2 \approx 82\).

Ordering rules. Programmes the model scored come first, by score. A programme is listed under weaker fit if its fit is below 40, or if two independent reviewers rate its relevance below 2 on a 1–5 scale on average. Programmes the model did not score (for example when the free quota is exhausted) follow under their own heading, in similarity order, because a similarity-only number is not on the same footing as a fit score.

The weights 0.7 and 0.3 are design choices, not learned from data: no outcome data existed to learn them from. The ranker can only re-order; it can never add or remove a programme. See Layer 3.

docs.title: 8 · Verifying facts with a jury: majority voting
docs.text:
In plain words

A single language model checking a fact can be wrong, and it can share blind spots with the model that extracted the fact. So every claim is put to a panel of three models from three different companies, none of them from the extractor's company, and a claim is shown only if a majority agrees it is on the page. A jury of independent people is more reliable than any one of them; the same holds for models, provided their mistakes are independent.

The maths. If each judge is right with probability \(p\) and the judges err independently, a majority of three is right with probability

\[ P(\text{majority correct}) \;=\; p^3 + 3p^2(1-p) \]

(all three right, or exactly two right). This exceeds \(p\) whenever \(p > 0.5\), which is Condorcet's jury theorem.

Worked example

Three judges, each 80% accurate and independent: \(0.8^3 + 3 \times 0.8^2 \times 0.2 = 0.512 + 0.384 = 0.896\). The panel is right about 90% of the time, better than any single judge. If the three judges always made the same mistakes, the panel would be no better than one judge, which is why we use judges from different companies.

The decision rule. A claim is confirmed only if both conditions hold:

\[ \text{confirmed} \;=\; \underbrace{\text{located on the page}}_{\text{plain code}} \;\wedge\; \underbrace{\text{at least 2 of 3 judges agree}}_{\text{language models}} \]

The first condition is checked by code at no model cost: the claim's date, amount or quote must actually be found on the page. A claim that fails either condition is not shown as fact; the card says "not stated, see the official page".

LocateCode searches the page for the claimed date, amount or quote. InterpretThree judges from three companies read only that passage and vote. DecideLocated and a 2-of-3 majority: shown. Otherwise withheld.

See Layer 0.

docs.title: 9 · Measuring agreement: Fleiss' kappa
docs.text:
In plain words

If three judges agree 90% of the time, is that impressive? Not if 90% of claims are obviously true, because they would agree that often by chance. Fleiss' kappa measures agreement beyond what chance alone would produce: 1 is perfect agreement, 0 is no better than chance.

The maths. For \(N\) items, each rated by \(n\) judges into categories \(j\), with \(n_{ij}\) the number of judges who put item \(i\) in category \(j\):

\[ \kappa \;=\; \frac{\bar{P} - \bar{P}_e}{1 - \bar{P}_e},\qquad \bar{P} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\frac{\sum_j n_{ij}^2 - n}{n(n-1)},\qquad \bar{P}_e = \sum_j p_j^2,\quad p_j = \frac{\sum_i n_{ij}}{Nn} \]

\(\bar{P}\) is the observed agreement and \(\bar{P}_e\) the agreement expected by chance from how often each category is used overall.

In ACCESS. Over 1,888 rule judgements, \(\kappa = 0.51\), "moderate" on the Landis and Koch scale [15]. Some disagreement is healthy here: three judges who always agreed would suggest they share the same blind spots, which is exactly what the panel is meant to avoid.

κ Landis and Koch label 0.00–0.20 slight 0.21–0.40 fair 0.41–0.60 moderate 0.61–0.80 substantial 0.81–1.00 almost perfect

docs.title: 10 · Testing the tester: fault injection and confidence intervals
docs.text:
In plain words

How do we know the verification catches errors? We plant errors on purpose (a deadline moved by months, an amount multiplied by four, a nationality rule reversed) and count how many are caught. Because we know where every planted error is, the catch rate can be measured directly. Small samples are uncertain, so each rate comes with a range of plausible values: the 95% confidence interval.

The maths. For \(k\) errors caught out of \(n\) planted, the detection rate is \(\hat{p} = k/n\). We report the Wilson score interval, which behaves well for small samples and for rates near 0% or 100%:

\[ \frac{\hat{p} + \dfrac{z^2}{2n} \;\pm\; z\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n} + \dfrac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1 + \dfrac{z^2}{n}}, \qquad z = 1.96 \text{ for 95\%} \]

Worked examples from ACCESS

  • Re-worded amount check, correct amounts accepted: 35 of 44 → 80%, interval 66–89%.
  • Negative control, deliberately wrong amounts accepted: 1 of 28 → 4%, interval 0.6–18%.
  • Harvester filter, real programme pages wrongly discarded: 6 of 60 → 10%, interval 5–20%.

The width of the interval is the honest part: with 60 pages we can say the miss rate is somewhere between about one page in twenty and one in five, not that it is exactly 10%.

For search quality we use a bootstrap interval instead: the 100 benchmark queries are resampled 2,000 times and the middle 95% of the resulting scores is reported. See Layer 0 and the test report.

docs.title: 11 · How search quality is measured: recall@k and MRR
docs.text:
In plain words

We took 100 programmes at random and had a model from a different company write the query a qualifying researcher might type, without naming the programme. Each query has exactly one right answer, so we can ask: did the right programme appear in the first five results (recall@5)? And how close to the top was it, on average (MRR)?

The maths. For \(Q\) queries, with \(\text{rank}_q\) the position of the correct programme for query \(q\):

\[ \text{Recall@}k = \frac{1}{Q}\sum_{q=1}^{Q} \mathbb{1}\left[\text{rank}_q \le k\right] \qquad \text{MRR} = \frac{1}{Q}\sum_{q=1}^{Q} \frac{1}{\text{rank}_q} \]

\(\mathbb{1}[\cdot]\) is 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise.

Worked example

Four queries whose correct programmes appear at positions 1, 3, 7 and 2. Recall@5 \(= 3/4 = 0.75\) (position 7 misses the top five). MRR \(= (1 + \tfrac{1}{3} + \tfrac{1}{7} + \tfrac{1}{2})/4 \approx 0.49\).

ACCESS reaches recall@5 = 0.93 and MRR = 0.79 with the method in use. See Layer 2.

docs.title: 12 · Answering questions from the official page: retrieval-augmented generation
docs.text:
In plain words

A language model asked "Do I need work experience?" might answer from general knowledge, which can be wrong for this particular programme. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) first finds the relevant passages of the programme's own page and then requires the model to answer only from them, quoting them word for word. If the passages do not answer the question, the model must say so.

flowchart LR
  P[Official page text] --> C[Split into passages<br/>110 words, 30 overlapping]
  Q[Researcher's question] --> R
  C --> R[Retrieve the best 4 passages<br/>BM25 + embeddings, fused by RRF]
  R --> M[Model answers only from<br/>these passages, citing P1–P4<br/>and quoting word for word]
  M --> V{Every quote found<br/>on the page?}
  V -- yes --> A[Answer shown as verified]
  V -- no --> X[Answer flagged as not verified]
  M -. nothing relevant .-> N["'The official page does not say.'"]

Swipe sideways to see the whole diagram.

Why passages overlap. With 110-word windows that step forward by 80 words, a sentence cut at one boundary appears whole in the next passage.

The quote check. A quote counts as found if it appears on the page word for word, or if at least 60% of its four-word runs do, which tolerates line breaks and punctuation differences without accepting invented text.

In ACCESS. 24 of 24 answers on a fixed question set were faithful (every quote on the page, every citation to a retrieved passage); 42% were "The official page does not say". See Layer 3.

docs.title: 13 · The trust score: a transparent weighted sum
docs.text:
In plain words

Each verified programme carries a single trust number that summarises why it can be trusted. It is a weighted average of six checks, each between 0 and 1, so anyone can see how it was built.

\[ \text{trust} = 0.25\,\text{authenticity} + 0.20\,\text{funding vote} + 0.20\,\text{rule support} + 0.20\,\text{grounding} + 0.10\,\text{agreement} + 0.05\,\text{validation} \] Component What it measures Authenticity Half for an official source (halved again for an archived copy or a certificate warning), half for the share of judges who agree the page describes this programme Funding vote Share of judges who agree the page is a funding opportunity Rule support Share of all judge votes on the eligibility rules that support them Grounding Share of the record's quotes found on the page (the quote check in section 12) Agreement Share of rules on which every judge voted the same way, discounted to 80% if fewer than three judges answered Validation 1 if the record passed its consistency checks, 0.5 if it raised an issue

The weights are expert choices; the Auditor's labelled test results could later be used to learn them.

docs.title: 14 · Sharing a free quota fairly: rate budgets
docs.text:
In plain words

Every model provider caps how many words (tokens) each model accepts per minute and per day. Background verification would happily use all of it, leaving a waiting researcher stuck in a queue. So the quota is divided: background work may use at most 60% of each minute's allowance, and the rest is reserved for live searches.

The maths. For a model with a per-minute limit \(L\), the most a role may use in any minute is

\[ \text{cap}_{\text{role}} \;=\; L \times s \times \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{live searches}\\ 0.6 & \text{background verification} \end{cases} \]

where \(s = 0.85\) is a safety factor that keeps retries and rough token estimates from tipping usage over the provider's limit. Daily budgets are split by role in the same way over a rolling 24-hour window.

The consequence. Verification speed is set by free quotas, not computing power, which is why the verified library grows by tens of programmes a day. See Models and resources.

docs.title: Layer 0 · Building the library
docs.text:
Layer 0 runs offline and continuously. It turns web pages into verified programme records: structured descriptions of funding programmes in which every displayed fact has been checked against the funder's own page. Because it runs in the background, slow and careful verification never delays a user's search.

1 · HarvesterFinds and fetches funder pages; discards irrelevant ones cheaply 2 · NormalizerExtracts each programme into a fixed schema, with a quote per fact 3 · Info CriticVerifies each fact with a three-company judge panel 4 · LibraryVector index (meaning) and rule register (eligibility rules)

The Auditor tests the Info Critic with planted errors, and the Sentinel monitors the whole pipeline.

The maths behind this layer

Plain-language explanations, equations and worked examples: majority voting, Fleiss' kappa, fault injection and confidence intervals and the trust score.

docs.title: The funnel
docs.text:
Pages fetched

141,740

Programme records extracted6,090 Fully verified629 From 7,821 websites, as of 31 October 2026. Bars are not to scale.

Most fetched pages are not funding programmes (27,496) or are duplicates (6,025). About 18,900 further candidate pages are waiting to be read by the Normalizer. We chose to verify existing records before extracting more: a smaller library in which every row is checked is more useful than a larger one that cannot be trusted.

docs.title: 1 · Harvester
docs.text:
What it does. Finds funding websites, fetches their pages, renders pages that are built by JavaScript, and keeps pages that look like a single funding programme.

Method.

  • Prioritised sources. National and government scholarship schemes first, then universities in ranking order (QS World University Rankings 2026), starting from each university's central scholarships page. Within the priority countries, the country with the fewest verified programmes is served next, so a large queue for one country cannot starve another (max-min fairness).
  • Polite crawling. robots.txt is respected, one request per website at a time, with delays and back-off. Sites that block automated access are read from the Internet Archive instead, labelled with the snapshot date; protection is never circumvented.
  • A free keyword filter scores each page before any language model sees it. This is the cascade principle: the model quota is the scarcest resource.
  • Duplicate detection by a fingerprint of each page's text (SHA-256 hash).
  • A headless browser (Playwright) renders pages whose content only appears after JavaScript runs.

Why this method. The state of the art for targeted crawling is focused crawling with a learned link classifier. We did not use it: it needs labelled training links, and the bottleneck is the extraction quota, not crawling, so a smarter crawler would not increase the number of verified records per day.

Evidence (crawl log, one row per request, 7 October):

Measure Value Fetched successfully 72% of 84,415 requests Skipped because robots.txt disallows 501 requests Pages passed to the Normalizer that were real programmes (precision) 67% (1,762 of 2,612) …that were index pages listing programmes (used for their links) 25% …that were irrelevant 7% Real programmes the filter discarded (miss rate), random sample of 60 10% (95% CI 5–20%)

Where it fails. The filter misses about one programme page in ten. Of the six misses in the sample, two scored just under the threshold, two were not in English, and two were old news items. Adding foreign-language keywords rescued none of the six and let three irrelevant pages through, so it was reverted: the misses fail on page structure, not vocabulary. Lowering the threshold would raise recall, but recall is not the bottleneck while thousands of pages wait for extraction.

docs.title: 2 · Normalizer
docs.text:
What it does. A language model reads each candidate page and fills a fixed schema of about 50 typed fields: programme type, career levels, host country, deadline, amount, coverage of tuition and travel, and eligibility rules.

Method. Zero-shot, schema-constrained information extraction with Google Gemini. "Zero-shot" means the model is given instructions and the schema, but no training examples. Each eligibility rule is stored as a typed triple, for example nationality in [Singapore, Singapore PR], marked as hard or soft, and every field must carry a word-for-word quote from the page. The quote is what later makes the fact checkable.

Example of a verified record (LKY-STEP Award, Singapore):

Field Value Quote from the page Nationality Singapore citizen or permanent resident "Be Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents." Amount 3,500 SGD, one-time "One-time cash award of S$3,500." Career level Undergraduate "Be matriculating into a full-time undergraduate degree course…" Verification Each rule confirmed by 3 of 3 judges

Why this method. A fine-tuned extractor would need labelled training data, which does not exist for this task; hand-written parsers break across thousands of different site layouts. Zero-shot extraction generalises across layouts with no training data.

Trade-off. The free tier allows roughly 500 pages per day, which is the main limit on throughput. A rule the page states but the model misses cannot be enforced; the Q&A feature (Layer 3) can still surface it from the page text.

docs.title: The host-country field
docs.text: Originally, programmes held in more than one country were labelled with a single value, "Multiple". Search treated this as a wildcard, so such programmes appeared under every country filter. The field now holds an explicit list of countries or regions, a flag for programmes open to any destination, and a supporting quote, all verified like any other claim. A list the judges cannot confirm becomes "not stated", which remains visible to every search rather than hiding the programme. The effect on a search for Japan: about 156 results before, 94 after.

docs.title: 3 · Info Critic
docs.text:
What it does. Decides what a user is allowed to see. It verifies each record in two stages and publishes only records whose displayed facts are all confirmed.

Method.

A · Whole recordThree judges: is this page a funding programme, and does the record describe it? B1 · LocateCode finds each claim's quote, date or amount on the page. Not found means not confirmed, at zero model cost. B2 · InterpretThree judges see only the located passage and vote on one claim at a time. C · DecideA majority confirms: the claim is shown. Otherwise it is withheld as "not stated".

The claims checked are each eligibility rule, the deadline, the amount, "fully funded", the programme type and the host country. A record is verified only if every claim it shows is confirmed and at least one eligibility rule is confirmed.

  • An ensemble of heterogeneous judges. The judge pool holds six models from six companies (OpenAI, Alibaba, NVIDIA, Zhipu, Microsoft and Meta). Each record is judged by three of them, from three different companies, and never by the extractor's company (Google). A record is never decided by fewer than three judges; it waits.
  • Claim decomposition, following FActScore [9]: a whole-record verdict hides which part is wrong, so each claim is checked separately.
  • Locate, then interpret. For dates and amounts, exact matching on the page is free and more reliable than a model's reading, so it runs first. The judges then answer a narrow question about one passage, with known traps listed (for example, an intake date is not a deadline; a range is not a single value).

Why this method. A single strong judge is cheaper but shows known biases [4], [12]. A majority vote outperforms its members only if their errors are independent (Condorcet's jury theorem); judges from different companies are less likely to share blind spots [11].

Evidence.

  • Agreement between judges: Fleiss' κ = 0.51 over 1,888 rule judgements [14], "moderate" on the Landis and Koch scale [15]. Some disagreement is expected from independent judges; near-perfect agreement would suggest an echo chamber.
  • Why stage B was added: measured on 575 records, whole-record judging was wrong in both directions. It marked 93% of correct deadlines and 91% of correct amounts as unconfirmed, yet caught only 27% of planted deadline errors and 21% of planted amount errors (see the Auditor below).
  • Locate step, all records, no model cost: true claims located: deadline 85%, amount 92%, rule quote 98%. Planted wrong deadlines were located in only 0.5% of cases and inflated amounts in 0%, so they are caught before any judge reads them.

Trade-offs. Three extra short judge calls per record mean about 40% fewer records verified per day on free quota. Exact matching can miss a true value written in an unusual format; the cost is a withheld claim, never a wrong one shown.

docs.title: A wording effect, measured with a control
docs.text: Judges rejected correct amounts when the claim said "the programme pays X" and the page said "up to X". After the claim was reworded to accept a stated maximum, 35 of 44 previously rejected amounts were confirmed. Because loosening a check could also let wrong values through, we ran a negative control: deliberately wrong amounts on the same pages. Only 1 of 28 was accepted, and that value matched a real award tier on the page.

docs.title: Trust score
docs.text: Each verified record also receives a transparent trust score: a weighted sum of source authenticity (0.25), funding vote (0.20), rule support (0.20), grounding of quotes (0.20), judge agreement (0.10) and validation checks (0.05). The weights are expert choices, not learned, because no labelled outcomes existed at design time. The Auditor's test results provide labelled data from which the weights could later be learned.

docs.title: 4 · Auditor
docs.text:
What it does. Measures the Info Critic instead of trusting it.

Method. Fault injection, also known as mutation testing [16]: take a verified record, insert one known error, and run it through verification exactly as deployed. Because the location of the error is known, the detection rate can be measured directly. Five error types are planted: an invented eligibility rule, a flipped nationality rule ("open to" ↔ "not open to"), a deadline shifted by months, an amount multiplied by four, and a record paired with another programme's page. The Auditor also re-reads random pages blind and compares its extraction with the stored record. It is never one of the judges whose work it tests.

Evidence: whole-record panel alone, 768 planted errors.

Invented rule

100%

Wrong page98% Flipped nationality51% Shifted deadline27% Amount ×421% Share of planted errors caught. The panel reliably rejects invented content but often misses subtle changes, which motivated the claim-by-claim check.

The Auditor now tests the full verification process (panel and claim check together). In a pilot, the claim check caught 4 of 4 flipped nationality rules. Full-process detection rates per error type are still accumulating.

A bug found by the test itself. The first full-process test reported a planted amount as "missed". Inspection showed that the panel had already removed the amount from the record in place, so the test compared the planted value with nothing. The test now compares against a snapshot taken before judging.

docs.title: 5 · Sentinel
docs.text: Monitors progress every five minutes. It diagnoses problems with fixed rules first, and lets a language model choose only from a whitelist of safe actions: restart an agent, rest a failing model, change the number of workers. A health audit found that provider outages had been counted against the pages themselves, silently retiring 15,729 of 15,731 queued pages; provider failures now pause the work instead.

docs.title: Library: vector index and rule register
docs.text:
Verified records are published into two stores.

  • Vector index. Each programme is converted into an embedding with nomic-embed-text [19], run locally, and searched exhaustively by cosine similarity. Approximate indexes (such as HNSW) pay off only at around 100,000 vectors; at a few thousand programmes, exhaustive search takes milliseconds.
  • Rule register. A typed store of eligibility rules (attribute, operator, value, hard or soft, quote, judge votes) that the eligibility gate evaluates in Layer 2.

docs.title: Layer 1 · Understanding the user
docs.text:
Layer 1 turns a short form into a researcher profile. The profile mirrors the programme record: an embedding that represents the researcher's interests, and typed attributes that can be tested against eligibility rules.

flowchart LR
  F["Consent-based form<br/>interests · nationality · career stage<br/>target countries · programme types"] --> E["Interest embedding<br/>(for finding relevant programmes)"]
  F --> A["Eligibility attributes<br/>(for testing rules)"]

The maths behind this layer

Plain-language explanations, equations and worked examples: embeddings, field inference and the follow-up question.

docs.title: Input form: consent and data minimisation
docs.text:
What it does. Collects only what matching needs, after explicit consent.

Method.

  • The form states, next to the search button, that answers are used only to find funding and that searches are kept without a name to evaluate the system. Running a search signals consent.
  • Saved searches never store a personal name; they are kept only to evaluate the system.
  • A blank field means unknown, never "no" and never a default value. An early version used a default age of 25, which silently decided age rules for users who had never given an age; this was removed.

Why. Consent-based capture is part of the design, and data minimisation follows the principles of Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

docs.title: Profile builder
docs.text:
What it does. Converts the form into the two representations above.

Method. Facts from the form are used unchanged. Research fields are inferred locally by zero-shot embedding classification: the description and 24 field labels are embedded, and every field within a small margin (0.035) of the best cosine score is kept. The user can confirm or override the inferred fields.

Why this method. An earlier version used a cloud language model to build the profile, which made every search depend on the model's quota. The local method answers instantly and never fails because a provider is busy. A margin is used rather than the single best label because the top label alone was noisy (for one physicist, physics scored just below chemistry).

Evidence. The whole first-results path, including the profile, takes 0.02–0.3 s with no cloud AI.

docs.title: One follow-up question
docs.text:
What it does. After a search, ACCESS may ask one question, such as "How many years since your PhD?".

Method. The question is the missing attribute that appears in the most "unknown" eligibility checks across the results. Each unknown check is an uncertain outcome, so the attribute that occurs most often removes the most uncertainty per question: a greedy approximation of information gain.

Why. It is deterministic, free and asks one question at a time, instead of a long questionnaire up front or a conversational interviewer.

docs.title: Layer 2 · Matching and eligibility
docs.text:
Layer 2 answers two separate questions: which programmes are relevant to this researcher? and which of them is the researcher eligible for? The first is a search problem; the second is a logic problem. They are handled by different methods on purpose.

The maths behind this layer

Plain-language explanations, equations and worked examples: BM25, rank fusion, the eligibility gate and recall@k and MRR.

docs.title: Research matcher: hybrid search
docs.text:
What it does. Retrieves the programmes most relevant to the researcher's interests from the whole library.

Method. Two searches are combined:

  • Keyword search (BM25) [17] matches exact terms, such as "postdoctoral", a field name or a programme acronym.
  • Dense search compares embeddings [5], [19], so it also matches paraphrases ("funding for early-career researchers" and "postdoctoral fellowship").
  • Reciprocal rank fusion [18] merges the two ranked lists without having to put their scores on a common scale. Keyword results are weighted 2:1.

Why this method. Funding pages are full of exact names and acronyms, which favour keyword search; paraphrased queries favour dense search. A cross-encoder reranker could add accuracy but was not used: on a CPU it adds latency for marginal gains at this scale.

Evidence: known-item benchmark. 100 programmes were sampled at random. For each, a model from a different company than the embedder wrote the query a qualifying researcher might type, in its own words and without the programme's or funder's name. The programme is the single correct answer.

Dense only

73%

Keyword only (BM25)88% Hybrid, equal weights89% Hybrid, keyword 2:1 (used)93% Recall@5: share of queries whose target programme appears in the top five results. 95% confidence interval for the method used: 88–97%. Method Recall@1 Recall@5 Recall@10 MRR ms per query Dense only 0.49 0.73 0.83 0.60 11 Keyword only (BM25) 0.72 0.88 0.93 0.79 0.5 Hybrid, equal weights 0.66 0.89 0.94 0.76 12 Hybrid, keyword 2:1 0.69 0.93 0.94 0.79 14

A negative result: rewriting programme descriptions in plain English before embedding them did not improve dense search (MRR 0.59).

docs.title: Eligibility gate
docs.text:
What it does. Tests every rule of every candidate programme against the profile, one line at a time, and places each programme in one of three groups.

Method. Deterministic constraint satisfaction over the rule register. Each rule has one of five outcomes:

Outcome Meaning Pass The profile meets the rule Fail The profile does not meet the rule Near A soft rule is missed by a small margin (e.g. IELTS 0.5 below the requirement) Conditional Met once the current degree is completed Unknown The profile does not contain the attribute. Never treated as a pass EligibleNo rule fails. Passed on to ranking. Within reachOnly soft, closable gaps. Shown separately, easiest gap first. ExcludedA hard rule fails, for example nationality. Never shown as a match.

Why rules, not a model. The same input always gives the same answer, every decision can be traced to a quoted rule, and the logic can be tested. A language model deciding eligibility would be non-deterministic and hard to audit, and models are known to struggle with negation [6].

Evidence. 32 of 32 hand-checked unit tests (one per rule type and outcome) and 4 of 4 consistency checks pass, for example "a programme is never both eligible and excluded". The gate runs in under a millisecond per programme.

Where it fails. The gate is only as good as the rules it receives, which is why every rule is verified in Layer 0 first.

docs.title: Near-miss set
docs.text:
What it does. Shows programmes that the researcher narrowly misses, ordered by how much effort it would take to close the gap.

Method. Soft-constraint relaxation: hard rules (nationality, age, years since PhD) exclude; soft rules missed within a margin create a near miss. Near misses are ordered by an estimated gap cost in weeks, for example 0.5 IELTS points ≈ 4 weeks, one career step ≈ 26 weeks.

Limitation. The effort estimates are hand-set approximations. Near misses are also rare in practice, because funding pages seldom state numeric thresholds: a minimum GPA appears in 17 of 598 records and an IELTS score in 2.

docs.title: Layer 3 · Ranking and explanation
docs.text:
Layer 3 orders the eligible programmes by fit and explains each result. It follows one user-experience principle: answer first, then refine.

The maths behind this layer

Plain-language explanations, equations and worked examples: the fit score and retrieval-augmented generation.

0.4 s · Instant resultsSearch and eligibility gate. No cloud AI is involved, so results appear even if every model provider is down. ~15 s · Fit rankingIn the background, a language model scores each eligible programme for fit and gives a reason. On request · Plan and Q&AAn application plan, and answers to questions, each citing the official page.

docs.title: Fit ranker
docs.text:
What it does. Scores every eligible programme from 0 to 100 for fit with the researcher's field, career stage and goals, with a one-sentence reason.

Method. An LLM used as a ranker, scoring candidates in batches of ten, combined with semantic similarity by late fusion:

final score = 0.7 × fit score + 0.3 × semantic similarity (rescaled to 0–100)

Design safeguards.

  • The ranker only orders results. It can never add or remove a programme; the eligibility gate alone decides that.
  • If a model skips items, a second pass scores them. If the main model is unavailable, a fallback chain across three companies takes over. Each item records which model scored it, because scores from different models are not on the same scale.
  • Without any score, results stay in similarity order and are labelled as such. A score is never invented.

Why this method. The state of the art for LLM ranking is sliding-window listwise reranking, which needs several model calls per search; on a rate-limited free tier, batches of ten give context across candidates at a fraction of the calls. The 0.7 / 0.3 weights are expert choices, not learned.

Evidence. Initially, three or four of 30 programmes were left unranked and ranking took 215–531 s, because background verification filled the shared per-minute model quota. After batching and giving live requests priority over background work, one test persona had 29 of 29 programmes ranked in 55 s and another 17 of 17 in 15 s. The cost: background verification runs up to 40% slower.

docs.title: Online reviewers
docs.text: Two reviewers from different companies rate the relevance of the top 15 eligible results and five near misses. A low rating moves a result to the end, with the reason shown, but never removes it: in testing, one reviewer wrongly dropped a valid scholarship, and an eligible result must not disappear because of one model's opinion.

docs.title: Application plans and questions
docs.text:
What it does. For any programme, ACCESS can write an application plan or answer a question such as "Do I need work experience?".

Method. Retrieval-augmented generation [10], scoped to that programme's official page. The page is split into overlapping passages; the most relevant passages are retrieved with hybrid search; the model must answer only from those passages, cite them and copy quotes word for word. Every quote is then checked against the page text. If the passages do not contain the answer, the model must reply "The official page does not say."

Evidence. 24 of 24 answers to a fixed set of questions were faithful: every quote appeared on the page and every citation pointed to a retrieved passage (exact 95% lower bound 0.86). Median answer time 2.7 s. 42% of answers were "The official page does not say." This check proves the quotes are real; it does not test whether the answer follows logically from them.

A bug found by this evaluation. The first run scored 79%. Every rejected quote was in fact on the page: the checker did not recognise citations written as "P5" instead of "5". After the fix, the same answers scored 24 of 24.

docs.title: Literature review
docs.text: ACCESS draws on two strands of research: scholarly recommender systems, which match researchers to opportunities, and the verification of language-model output, which addresses whether the facts a model produces are correct. Three further findings shaped specific design choices.

docs.title: Scholarly recommender systems
docs.text:
Study Approach Key finding Limitation for our problem Zhang et al., 2023 [1] Survey of 225 scholarly recommender studies Content-based filtering dominates; most systems address a single task No integrated support across funding, careers and venues Zhu et al., 2023 [2] BERT model matching publication profiles to NIH grant announcements Semantic matching improves grant recommendation Suitability is treated as relevance; eligibility is not modelled Zhao et al., 2024 [3] Survey of LLM-based recommender systems LLMs build richer representations of users and items Extracted content is not verified against its source

The closest prior work, the NIH grant recommender [2], shows that semantic matching works for grants. However, semantic relevance does not establish suitability: an opportunity may depend on nationality, career stage, institutional affiliation or a deadline.

docs.title: Verifying what language models produce
docs.text: Study Finding Consequence in ACCESS Ji et al., 2023 [7] Generated text can be fluent yet unsupported by its source ("hallucination") No extracted fact is shown without verification Thorne et al., 2018 [8] FEVER: claims are verified against evidence as supported, refuted or not enough information Our three outcomes: confirmed, rejected, not stated Min et al., 2023 [9] FActScore: split long text into atomic facts and verify each separately Records are verified claim by claim, not as a whole Lewis et al., 2020 [10] Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in retrieved passages Judges and the Q&A feature see the relevant page passage Verga et al., 2024 [11] A panel of diverse smaller models judges better, and with less bias, than one large model Three judges from three different companies Panickssery et al., 2024 [12] LLM evaluators recognise and favour their own outputs The extracting model never judges its own work

docs.title: Findings that shaped specific design choices
docs.text: Finding Design consequence A single LLM acting as a judge shows position and self-enhancement bias [4] Verification by a panel with majority voting Sentence embeddings allow fast semantic search [5] A vector index to retrieve programmes by meaning Language models are largely insensitive to negation: "not open to international applicants" resembles "open to international applicants" [6] Eligibility is decided by deterministic rules, never by similarity scores

docs.title: Research gap
docs.text: No existing system combines (i) collection from the open web, (ii) verification of extracted facts against their source, (iii) eligibility as a hard constraint and (iv) personalised ranking. ACCESS integrates all four.

docs.title: Models and resources
docs.text: ACCESS uses only pretrained models, through free tiers or run locally. No model is trained or fine-tuned, and no paid service is used.

docs.title: No echo chamber
docs.text:
Each role is assigned so that no model grades its own work:

  • the extractor (Google) is never one of the judges;
  • each record's three judges come from three different companies;
  • the auditor's own votes are excluded when it re-checks records it judged;
  • the model that writes benchmark queries (NVIDIA) differs from the embedding model (Nomic).

docs.title: Working within free-tier limits
docs.text:
Free tiers cap how many requests and tokens each model accepts per minute and per day. ACCESS treats these limits as a scheduling problem:

  • Token budgets per role over a rolling 24-hour window, so background verification cannot use up the quota that live searches need.
  • Live requests first. Background roles may use only 60% of each minute's token allowance, so a researcher's search never queues behind background work.
  • A dedicated model for the hosted demo. Free-tier limits apply per model, so the hosted demo ranks with a model (GPT-OSS-20B, at low reasoning effort) that no background agent calls. Its whole per-minute and daily allowance goes to live searches: a search with 29 eligible programmes is scored in about 9 s. One model still allows only about one such search per minute; a search that waits longer than 30 s is shown in relevance order instead.
  • Fallback chains. Each AI role has an ordered list of models from different providers; the first with quota available is used.
  • Failures are never the record's fault. A provider outage, timeout or quota error pauses the work. It does not count against the page being processed.

The main consequence is speed: verification throughput is set by the slowest company's free quota, not by computing power. This is why the verified library grows by tens of records per day rather than thousands.
